## Basics of AI

Artificial intelligence tools — generative AI in particular — are now used throughout the research lifecycle, from literature search to software coding to editing manuscripts. This section is a primer on what AI actually is in a research context, where it can help, where it can get you into trouble, and how to disclose using it — adapted from Aalto University's institutional guidance on AI in research.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this section you will be able to:

- Distinguish AI as a topic, a method, and a tool in research, and explain why the "tool" framing is the one that applies to most researchers
- Identify where generative AI can help across the seven stages of the research lifecycle, using both a reference table and a figure
- Recognize the misconduct risks of fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism, and apply the rule of thumb for when AI output is safe to use
- Read a 2×2 matrix to judge how much you can safely delegate to AI, based on your own expertise and the stakes of the output
- Know when AI use must be disclosed under common publisher policy, and write a disclosure statement that meets that bar

:::

### What Is AI?

"AI" is a genuinely vague term, and a lot of confusion in research settings comes from people talking past each other because they mean different things by it. In a research context, AI can play three distinct roles, and it matters which one you're actually doing:

- **AI as a Topic** — studying AI itself: human–chatbot interaction, new machine learning algorithms, the societal impact of automation. Here, AI *is* the research question
- **AI as a Method** — using machine learning or other AI techniques as your analysis approach: classification, prediction, clustering. Here, AI is the instrument you use to answer a different research question
- **AI as a Tool** — using an application with an AI (often generative AI) component to assist a task that isn't itself about AI: proofreading a manuscript, debugging code, drafting an outline. Here, AI is closer to a very capable piece of software than to a research method

For the large majority of researchers — including those who neither study AI nor use it as a method — AI shows up in the third role. Even if your field has nothing to do with machine learning, you are still very likely to encounter generative AI as a tool sitting next to your text editor, your code, or your inbox. This chapter, and this book more broadly, focuses on exactly that: **generative AI as a tool** for research work, not as a research topic or method in its own right.

### Generative AI Across the Research Lifecycle

Generative AI tools can plausibly assist at every stage of the research process, not just the writing at the end. The table below gives concrete examples at each stage:

| Stage | Examples of AI assistance |
|---|---|
| Planning | Literature search, grant drafting, research question brainstorming |
| Data collection | Survey design, data synthesis, simulations |
| Pre-processing | Formatting, quality checks, data cleaning |
| Analysis | Analysis code generation, qualitative annotations |
| Preservation | Documentation, README generation, metadata |
| Sharing | Manuscript drafting, press releases, social media posts |
| Reuse | Code documentation, dataset descriptions |

The same stages are shown visually below, arranged around the research cycle with Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR) — ethics and law — placed deliberately at the center, since it applies to every stage rather than being a separate step of its own:

![The research process aided by AI tools, with Responsible Conduct of Research at its core. Each of the seven stages — Plan, Collect, Process, Analyse, Preserve, Share, Reuse — lists concrete examples of where generative AI can assist. (Source: Glerean & Silva, 2026, CC-BY; original cycle diagram from rdmkit.elixir-europe.org, "The data lifecycle")](images/ch01/ai-research-lifecycle.png){fig-alt="A circular diagram showing seven research lifecycle stages — Plan, Collect, Process, Analyse, Preserve, Share, Reuse — arranged around a central RCR (Responsible Conduct of Research, Ethics and Law) hub, with bullet-point examples of AI assistance next to each stage"}

It's worth being explicit about something the table and figure can't show on their own: **every one of these uses carries risk**, and no task is universally safe or universally reckless with AI — it depends on the context and on the judgment of the person using the tool. As a responsible researcher, your job is to evaluate that risk *before* deciding whether to proceed with a given task, for a given stage, with a given tool. If you're unsure, talk it through with peers rather than guessing, or simply skip AI for that specific task. The next two sections give you concrete ways to make that judgment call.

### Avoiding Research Misconduct

Used carelessly, generative AI can walk you straight into research misconduct — not through malicious intent, but because of how these systems actually work. There are three classic forms of misconduct that AI makes easy to stumble into:

- **Fabrication** — generative AI *hallucinates*: it produces sensible-looking text, references, statistics, and data that simply do not exist. This is not a rare glitch; it's a structural property of how these models generate text (see the [appendix on how LLMs work](appendix-llms-and-agents.qmd) for why)
- **Falsification** — generative AI tools do not reason the way humans do. They produce the statistically likely output given their training data and your input, which is a fundamentally different process from genuine reasoning about evidence. Using AI to produce research findings or interpret results therefore carries a high risk of false conclusions
- **Plagiarism** — generative AI output can be based directly on someone else's research results. Presenting that output as your own findings, without properly citing the original work, can constitute plagiarism even when you never consciously copied anything

A simple rule of thumb ties all three together:

> If you do not have the ability or the resources to verify the output of a GenAI system — by finding the citations it claims exist, by confirming that someone else's work is summarized correctly, by detecting plagiarized text or code, by independently checking the analysis — then you should not use that output beyond self-learning or brainstorming.

### Evaluating Risk: Expertise × Output-Risk

Not all AI use is equally risky, and treating every use case the same way is neither realistic nor useful. If you're unsure how cautious to be about a specific task, two factors do most of the work in answering that question:

- **Your expertise** on the specific task you're delegating to AI
- **The importance of the output** — will it be submitted for peer review, or is it something lower-stakes, like a workshop webpage?

Crossing those two factors gives a 2×2 matrix, with a concrete recommendation and worked example in each quadrant:

| | Low expertise | High expertise |
|---|---|---|
| **High risk**<br>*(peer-review submission: text, code, figures, references)* | Use AI only to **brainstorm**: ask it what sources to read, get keyword suggestions, then go read the real sources.<br><br>*Example: ask which statistical methods might fit your data, then go read about them yourself rather than trusting the AI's explanation.* | Use AI for **simple delegated tasks you can fully review**. Check everything as carefully as if you had retyped it yourself — this is where overconfidence is most dangerous.<br><br>*Example: generating short code snippets function-by-function; asking AI to mark suggested text changes in bold so you decide which to apply manually.* |
| **Low risk**<br>*(event webpage, social media post, presentation)* | Use AI, but **accept a non-zero chance of errors** slipping through.<br><br>*Example: getting help with CSS for a workshop webpage, or "vibe-coding" a small demo.* | **Delegate most of the work to AI.** Verify that the output makes sense.<br><br>*Example: generating documentation for scripts you already wrote, or drafting a presentation outline from a transcript of your own recording.* |

A few notes on reading this matrix:

- The sensitivity of your *data* raises the risk level on top of everything above — with confidential or personal data, you have to think not only about how you use a tool, but which tool you're allowed to use at all
- A special case is generated software code where correctness can be formally checked with automated unit tests: if the tests are well-designed and actually cover the relevant behavior, this can lower the effective risk level — but it shifts the quality bar onto the tests themselves, which now need to be trustworthy
- Some situations won't fit neatly into any of the four quadrants. You remain the person ultimately responsible for judging whether a given use of AI is appropriate — the matrix is a starting heuristic, not a substitute for that judgment

### Disclosing AI Use

Disclosure expectations for AI use are grounded in the same four principles as research integrity generally: reliability, honesty, respect, and accountability (per the ALLEA European Code of Conduct). In practice, this comes down to two concrete questions when preparing a manuscript: *does this need to be declared*, and *if so, how*?

**What to declare.** Using Elsevier's publisher guidance as a representative example (always check your own target journal's or funder's specific policy first):

- **No declaration needed** — fixing typos and grammar only
- **Declaration required** — any synthesis of text, generation of code, creation of figures, suggestion of analysis approaches, or drafting of any section
- **AI-generated images** — acceptable only for illustrating a pipeline or method; never as result figures or quantitative plots

**Disclosure template.** When declaring AI use, a statement along these lines is the common pattern across publisher policies:

> **Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process.** During the preparation of this work, the author(s) used [NAME OF TOOL / SERVICE] in order to [REASON]. After using this tool/service, the author(s) reviewed and edited the content as needed and take(s) full responsibility for the content of the published article.

The line between "just grammar" and "substantive enough to disclose" is not always obvious in practice — a tool that reflows a sentence's structure or reorganizes a paragraph has crossed further than a spell-checker, even if it never introduced a factual claim. When in doubt, disclose.

::: {.callout-note}
## Takeaways

- AI in research is a tool, a method, or a topic — know which role it's playing; for most researchers, most of the time, it's a tool
- Generative AI can plausibly help at every stage of the research lifecycle, from planning through reuse — not just at the writing stage
- Fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism are the three ways careless AI use turns into research misconduct; verify anything you can't personally stand behind
- Use the expertise × output-risk matrix to calibrate how much you delegate: brainstorm-only in the high-risk/low-expertise quadrant, full delegation only in the low-risk/high-expertise one
- Disclose substantive AI use under common publisher policy — grammar-only fixes are the one clear exception, and when in doubt, disclose anyway
:::
